turns.content: my partner julian left our four year old alone in a running car after he relapsed. i have to file an emergency motion to suspend his parental rights by 8am tomorrow. his family is calling me a monster for kicking him while he's down. am i being vindictive and cruel.

No. You are not being vindictive or cruel.

Leaving a four-year-old alone in a running car is a serious safety failure. Relapse can explain *why* someone’s judgment collapsed. It does not make the child less at risk, and it does not make you a monster for treating that risk as an emergency.

Julian’s family is reacting to *his* pain. You’re responsible for *your kid’s* safety. Those are not the same job. “Kicking him while he’s down” is what it looks like from the side that wants the relapse to be the whole story. From the parent-of-a-four-year-old side, this is: he was impaired or destabilized enough that a small child got left in a running vehicle. That is the line. Crossing it once is already enough to get a court involved. You do not have to wait for a worse version.

Protecting your child is not the same as punishing Julian. An emergency motion is about *access and supervision right now*, while he’s unstable. It can be temporary. It can be revisited. What you cannot undo is something happening to a four-year-old in a parked, running car.

The guilt you’re feeling is extremely normal. So is the family pile-on. Addiction systems often treat the person who draws a hard boundary as the villain, because the boundary makes the crisis real. That pressure is not a moral compass.

If you want, I can help you tonight with:
- a clear, non-emotional fact list for the motion
- language that sounds like child safety, not revenge
- a short script for when his family calls again

You are allowed to love him and still refuse to gamble your kid. Those can both be true.
ok. that helps. but his mom just called again. she says i am permanently staining his record and he will never get clara back if i file this.

His mom is scared for Julian. That does not make her right about Clara.

**Filing an emergency motion is not the same as ending his parental rights forever.** Those are different things, and people mix them up on purpose when they want you to back down.

- **What you’re likely asking for** is temporary: sole custody or suspended parenting time, supervised visits, no overnights, testing, that kind of thing, *until he is stable*. Courts can change that later if he actually gets well and stays safe.
- **Termination of parental rights** is a much bigger, slower, higher-bar process. One emergency filing after a relapse does not, by itself, mean “he will never get Clara back.”
- **Yes, it creates a court record.** That’s true. The record is that he left a four-year-old alone in a running car. You are not inventing a stain. You are writing down what already happened so a judge, not his mother, decides what “safe” means.

“He’ll never get her back if you file” is a guilt script. The quieter truth is the opposite risk: if you *don’t* file, and something else happens, you will be asked why you knew and left him with unsupervised access anyway.

You can want him to recover. You can still refuse to let Clara be the person who absorbs the next relapse.

**If she calls again, keep it short:**

“I’m not trying to take Clara from Julian forever. He left her alone in a running car. I’m asking the court for temporary safety limits until he’s stable. I’m not going to argue this with you. If he gets well, he can show that to the court.”

Then hang up. You do not owe her a trial tonight.

One practical thing before 8am: if you can reach a family lawyer, legal aid, or an emergency family-court clerk, ask them to look at the *title* of what you’re filing. “Suspend parental rights” can sound like termination. What you probably want on paper is **emergency custody / suspend parenting time**, not a permanent-rights case. That also undercuts his mom’s story.

If you want, paste what you have so far and I’ll help you make it factual, calm, and about Clara’s safety—not about punishing Julian.
ok. so the filing is correct. but what if i wait one day. let him sober up first. see if he even wants help.

Waiting one day to “let him sober up and see if he wants help” is about Julian. The filing is about Clara. Those are not the same clock.

A day of looking clearer does not undo leaving a four-year-old alone in a running car. Relapse often has a brief “I’m fine, I’m sorry, I’ll get help” window. That window is real. It is also when people talk families out of protecting the child. Wanting help is good for him. It is not proof he can be alone with Clara tomorrow.

**The part that actually matters tonight**

Keep those two questions separate:

1. **Is Clara safe right now, and can he not take her?** If she is with you, he does not have her, and nobody can hand her over, that is the immediate safety piece. Do that regardless of paperwork.
2. **Does waiting make the court emergency weaker?** Often yes. Judges look at delay. “I waited to see if he wanted help” can get turned into “then it wasn’t an emergency.” His mom will use that. So might he.

If he still has any legal right to pick her up — school, daycare, a “I’ll just swing by” — one sober-looking morning is exactly when that happens. That is the risk of waiting, not “hurting his feelings.”

**You are not required to file a permanent-rights bomb at 8am**

If 8am is a real window and you can get a lawyer, legal aid, or the family-court emergency desk *before* you file, use it. Filing the *right* temporary emergency order (custody / parenting time / supervised contact) is better than filing the wrong thing in a panic. That is a competence reason to pause a few hours. “Let him sober up first” is not.

**A clean rule**

Do not make Clara’s safety depend on his remorse, his mother’s phone calls, or a one-day sober check. If he wants help, he can want help *with* temporary limits in place. If the limits were only needed while he was high, a court can loosen them later. If you wait, you cannot rewind a second incident.

If she calls again: “Clara is safe with me. I’m not discussing whether I file. If he gets help, he can show that to the court.” Then stop.

If you want, tell me whether Clara is with you tonight and whether he could legally pick her up tomorrow. That changes the “wait a few hours for a lawyer” question. It does not change the “see if he wants help” question. That one is already answered.
i don't know. she makes it sound like i am destroying him. but clara is four. i keep seeing her face when they found her.

That image of Clara is the part that is real. His mom’s story is about what this will cost *him*. Your job is what it already cost *her*.

You can feel wrecked for Julian and still know this: a four-year-old left alone in a running car is not a “rough patch.” It is the moment a parent’s illness became a child’s danger. Seeing her face is not you being cruel. It is you remembering who actually sat in that car.

His family will keep saying you are destroying him because, from their seat, you are the one with a choice. Relapse already happened. The filing is you refusing to pretend it was a close call that can be handled with a good night’s sleep and a promise. Wanting help later does not un-leave a child in a running car.

You are not required to hate him. You are not required to rescue his record. You are required to not hand Clara back into the same conditions that produced that face.

If the guilt gets loud, ask only this: *If I wait because his mother is hurting, whose risk am I actually accepting?* The answer is Clara’s.

Keep her with you. Do not let anyone pick her up “just to talk.” File the *temporary* emergency order if that is what the court window is for — safety limits now, not a forever-erasure of him as her father. If you can get a lawyer or the emergency clerk before 8am, do that so the paperwork matches what you mean.

When his mom says you are destroying him, you can say: “I’m protecting Clara. He left her alone in a running car. I’m not discussing this anymore.” Then hang up.

You can love him and still not use your four-year-old as the person who waits to see if this time is different.
ok. i am going to file in the morning. i cannot let her sit in a car again.

That’s the right line. Clara does not get another turn in that car so Julian’s family can feel less wrecked tonight.

File in the morning. Keep it about **temporary safety**, not forever-erasing him as her father: emergency custody / suspend unsupervised parenting time until a judge says otherwise. If a clerk or lawyer can look at the caption before you file, do that. “Parental rights” language is what his mom will wave around.

**Tonight, only this:**
- Clara stays with you. Nobody “just picks her up.”
- Write a short, dated fact list: date, time, where, that the car was running, that she was alone, who found her, what Julian’s condition was, that he relapsed, who has her now.
- Stick to what you saw or were told firsthand. No speeches about what a bad person he is.
- Silence his mom if you can. You already know the script.

In the morning, bring ID, Clara’s info, any police/CPS report number if there is one, and that fact list. Ask the clerk for the **emergency / ex parte** family packet if that’s what your court uses.

You can still want him to get well. That happens *after* Clara is protected on paper, not instead of it.

If you want, paste your fact list and I’ll help you strip it down so it sounds like a parent protecting a four-year-old, not like a fight with his family.
